entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6371"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 78</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.78.1-Ps.78.72">Psa 78:1-72</reference>. This Psalm appears to have been occasioned by the removal of the sanctuary from Shiloh in the tribe of Ephraim to Zion in the tribe of Judah, and the coincident transfer of pre-eminence in Israel from the former to the latter tribe, as clearly evinced by David's settlement as the head of the Church and nation. Though this was the execution of God's purpose, the writer here shows that it also proceeded from the divine judgment on Ephraim, under whose leadership the people had manifested the same sinful and rebellious character which had distinguished their ancestors in Egypt.</title> <div sID="gen9762" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6371"/><hi type="bold">1. my people ... my law--</hi>the language of a religious teacher (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.2">Psa 78:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.14">La 3:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.2.16">Ro 2:16</reference>, 27; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.49.4">Psa 49:4</reference>). The history which follows was a "dark saying," or riddle, if left unexplained, and its right apprehension required wisdom and attention. <div eID="gen9762" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: PSALM 78 Psa 78:1-72 . Though this was the execution of God's purpose, the writer here shows that it also proceeded from the divine judgment on Ephraim, under whose leadership the people had manifested the same sinful and rebellious character which had distinguished their ancestors in Egypt. 1. my people ... my law-- the language of a religious teacher ( Psa 78:2 ; La 3:14 ; Ro 2:16 , 27; compare Psa 49:4 ). The history which follows was a "dark saying," or riddle, if left unexplained, and its right apprehension required wisdom and attention.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6375"/><div sID="gen9767" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6375"/>9-11. The privileges of the first-born which belonged to Joseph (<reference osisRef="1Chr.5.1">1Ch 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.2">2</reference>) were assigned to Ephraim by Jacob (<reference osisRef="Gen.48.1">Ge 48:1</reference>). The supremacy of the tribe thus intimated was recognized by its position (in the marching of the nation to Canaan) next to the ark (<reference osisRef="Num.2.18-Num.2.24">Nu 2:18-24</reference>), by the selection of the first permanent locality for the ark within its borders at Shiloh, and by the extensive and fertile province given for its possession. Traces of this prominence remained after the schism under Rehoboam, in the use, by later writers, of Ephraim for Israel (compare Ho 5:3-14; 11:3-12). Though a strong, well-armed tribe, and, from an early period, emulous and haughty (compare <reference osisRef="Josh.17.14">Jos 17:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.8.1-Judg.8.3">Jud 8:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.41">2Sa 19:41</reference>), it appears, in this place, that it had rather led the rest in cowardice than courage; and had incurred God's displeasure, because, diffident of His promise, though often heretofore fulfilled, it had failed as a leader to carry out the terms of the covenant, by not driving out the heathen (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.24">Ex 23:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.31.16">De 31:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.15">2Ki 17:15</reference>). <div eID="gen9767" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 9-11. The privileges of the first-born which belonged to Joseph ( 1Ch 5:1 , 2 ) were assigned to Ephraim by Jacob ( Ge 48:1 ). The supremacy of the tribe thus intimated was recognized by its position (in the marching of the nation to Canaan) next to the ark ( Nu 2:18-24 ), by the selection of the first permanent locality for the ark within its borders at Shiloh, and by the extensive and fertile province given for its possession. Traces of this prominence remained after the schism under Rehoboam, in the use, by later writers, of Ephraim for Israel (compare Ho 5:3-14; 11:3-12). Though a strong, well-armed tribe, and, from an early period, emulous and haughty (compare Jos 17:14 ; Jud 8:1-3 ; 2Sa 19:41 ), it appears, in this place, that it had rather led the rest in cowardice than courage; and had incurred God's displeasure, because, diffident of His promise, though often heretofore fulfilled, it had failed as a leader to carry out the terms of the covenant, by not driving out the heathen ( Ex 23:24 ; De 31:16 ; 2Ki 17:15 ).

navigation_sections.title: Psa 78:1-72 . This Psalm appears to have been occasioned by the removal of the sanctuary from Shiloh in the tribe of Ephraim to Zion in the tribe of Judah, and the coincident transfer of pre-eminence in Israel from the former to the latter tribe, as clearly evinced by David's settlement as the head of the Church and nation. Though this was the execution of God's purpose, the writer here shows that it also proceeded from the divine judgment on Ephraim, under whose leadership the people had manifested the same sinful and rebellious character which had distinguished their ancestors in Egypt.
